title: Propeller-based Underwater Piezoelectric Energy Harvesting System for an Autonomous IoT Sensor System
venue: Journal of the Korean Physical Society

sections.heading: Propeller-based Underwater Piezoelectric Energy Harvesting System for an Autonomous IoT Sensor System
sections.text:
Sebin , ∗ Jae Yong , ∗ Deok Hwan , ∗ Wonseop , Yewon  and Se Yeong Cho Jeon Hwang SongDepartment of Electrical Engineering, Hanyang University, Seoul 133-791, Korea

Sin Woo  and Hong Hee Department of Mechanical Engineering, Hanyang University, Seoul 133-791, Korea

Tae Hyun † Department of Electrical Engineering, Hanyang University, Seoul 133-791, Korea (Received 11 November 2019; revised 12 December 2019; accepted 19 December 2019)

While there is a demand for energy harvesting in environments with water, such as rivers, lakes seas, it has been difficult to use energy harvesting, especially piezoelectricity, because of the waterproof problem and the low output scale. Here, we report a propeller-based underwater piezoelectric energy harvester consisting of a propeller, hitting sticks and a piezoelectric module. The hitting sticks spin with a rotating axis connected to a propeller rotated by water flow and hit a piezoelectric cantilever beam. Unlike previous tip mass method, a newly applied technique makes it possible to match a frequency by easily controlling the bending length of a piezoelectric module using an acrylic plate to find the maximum output power. For reliability, we performed an experiment at 1.2 $\mathrm { m } / \mathrm { s }$ , which is the actual water flow rate of the Han River in South Korea, and a frequency of 24.5 Hz occurred with four hitting sticks. The frequency-matched bending length was 80 mm (acrylic plate length: $1 0 ~ \mathrm { m m }$ ). Then, impedance matching was carried out: At a resistance of $1 0 . 8 \ \mathrm { k } \Omega$ , an output power of $1 7 \ \mathrm { m W _ { r m s } }$ and a power density of 57.4 mW/cm3 were obtained. This result is one of the highest results in a field of similar piezoelectric energy harvesting devices considering challenging conditions that occur in real environments. Finally, the system was applied to an LED light system, one of applications under water, and succeeded in operating a total of 972 LEDs with only one piezoelectric device. This research proves the potential and the feasibility of applying a piezoelectric energy harvesting system to a real underwater environment.

sections.heading: I. INTRODUCTION
sections.text:
With the increasing threat of climate change, it is becoming critical to produce energy that is cleaner and more environmentally friendly [1]. Energy academia and industry, which has been focusing on generating electricity with vast centralized power plants that run mostly on fossil fuels or nuclear energy, are now trying to diversify sources and methods of producing electrical energy, especially with renewable sources, exemplified by solar, wind, tidal and geothermal energy [2,3]. These attempts help reduce the use of fossil fuel and the carbon dioxide produced from the conventional coal- and gas-fired power plants, and contribute to securely providing electricity to consumers by overcoming intermittence, an implicit problem of renewable energy. As the Paris Agreement clearly states that the world should focus on minimizing greenhouse gas emission, renewables are the key to carbon-free power generation.

Not only are the sources of energy being changed, but the conventional centralized power generation is also being decentralized with an increasing importance of smart microgrids [3, 4]. This is the reason that micro power generation attracts more and more research interest; it enables an autonomous power supply to electronic devices and enables the establishment of an independent electricity grid in a remote area. One of the most prominent ways to generate micro power is energy harvesting, a technology that scavenges ambient energy and transforms it into a useful electrical energy [5–7]. It includes harvesting mechanical vibrations, sound waves, heat and light.

Among them, there are three possible methods to harvest mechanical energy: electromagnetics, electrostatics and piezoelectricity. While they all have their own pros and cons, the piezoelectricity boasts a wide range of power density and simple structures while emitting only a little electromagnetic interference [8, 9]. The direct piezoelectric effect occurs when a piezoelectric material is exposed to an external stress. As the material undergoes a volumetric change, the electric dipole in the solid becomes re-oriented and experiences an electric potential change in response to the exerted stress. The piezoelectric effect can be useful in many places with ambient mechanical energy and is thus applied to utilize unwanted machinery vibration. It can be also useful in generating electricity under a fluid flow with the help of a rotary mechanism that converts the flow into machinery movement. There have been some attempts to harvest wind energy with piezoelectric energy harvesters [10–12]. We can also use water flow as a source of piezoelectric energy harvesting.

Water flow is an energy resource that can be easily accessed wherever streams, rivers and oceans exist. In addition, because the rate of water flow is usually constant and reliable, it helps generate stable energy. It applies particularly to rivers and streams. Given that water has a relatively higher density than other common fluids, the energy density obtained using water flow is also higher. A piezoelectric energy harvester that utilizes fluid flow is an environment-friendly device; it does not produce any secondary environmental pollutants when converting water flow into energy.

Although studies on piezoelectric energy harvesting by water flow have been previously conducted, they suffered from a low output energy [13–15]. The highest output achieved in a piezoelectric energy harvesting experiment with a fluid flow involved the use of a windmill [10]. The experiment was performed with a propeller; the impact frequency was about 4.5 Hz and the maximum output was $1 . 0 4 ~ \mathrm { m W / c m ^ { 3 } }$ . With the water as the fluid, another experiment was conducted using a piezoelectric module at the flow of a vortex and turbulence. The resulting output was 0.07 mW/cm3, which was very low at a 100 Hz vibration [16]. It was difficult to use their power generation system as an energy source in a real underwater environment.

The aim of this paper is to introduce the possibility of utilizing water flow with piezoelectric technology in a small hydro power plant. In this experiment, we demonstrate that a piezoelectric energy harvester can generate substantial electricity using fluid flow. Until now, the amount of output energy from a piezoelectric energy harvester has been inadequate to generate electricity [16,17]. In this study, we harvested sufficient energy in a real underwater environment and to ultimately drive an actual LED application. Finally, we establish the possibility of an independent power source for an obstacle detection sensor under water, namely, the ultrasonic sensor shown in Fig. 1.

sections.heading: II. METHOD
sections.text:
Figure 2 shows that a piezoelectric module is composed of a piezoelectric plate and a stainless steel substrate plate (AISI Type 304SS). Two plates are completely attached with an epoxy-based glue with a compression process. The piezoelectric plate is made of eight ceramic thin sheets that form one plate. The thickness of the piezoelectric plate is 0.2 mm and that of the substrate is $1 . 3 5 \ \mathrm { m m }$ . For the experiment, the bending length, one of the variables in this study, is defined along the x-direction starting from line A. It is the length of the area in which bending of the module can occur. It can be adjusted as we attach a thick acrylic plate (thickness: 4 mm) with a large elastic modulus at the free end of the module where bending is not needed as a bending resistor. In the figure, B is the part where the module is fixed to the piezoelectric module holder, giving the module a cantilever structure. C is the 37 mm width of both the piezoelectric and the substrate plate whose widths are the same. The chemical formula of the piezoelectric plate is 0.4Pb(Ni1/3Nb2/3)O $^ 3$ -0.6Pb(Zr0.38Ti0.62)O $^ { 3 }$ . The material properties are as follows: a dielectric constant $\varepsilon _ { \mathrm { r } }$ of 2100, a piezoelectric charge constant $d _ { 3 1 }$ of $- 2 0 7 \ \times$ $1 0 ^ { - 1 2 }$ C/N, and Young’s modulus $\mathrm { E }$ of $6 . 3 \times 1 0 ^ { 1 0 }$ GPa in Table 1. Figure 3(a) shows the conceptual design of the propeller-based underwater piezoelectric energy harvester (PU-PEH) with hitting sticks rotated by a propeller. The piezoelectric module is installed as a cantilever structure in this experiment because the electric output of the piezoelectric plate depends on its $d _ { 3 1 }$ value [18–20]. Previous research on a piezoelectric cantilever structure revealed that the electric output depends on the amount of bending deflection per unit time [21,22]. Therefore, a higher impact force, deflection rate, spring constant of the module and hitting frequency are necessary to achieve a higher output [18,23,24]. Matching the hitting frequency from the hitting sticks to the piezoelectric module with the natural frequency of the module is also needed to achieve maximum output [25]. The flow rate of water was assumed to be constant, and so was the hitting frequency. Thus, in this study, the first natural frequency of the piezoelectric module was adjusted to match the hitting frequency of the hitting sticks, 24.5 Hz. To do so, we introduced a frequency matching technique to match the frequency to the piezoelectric module using a thick acrylic plate with an appropriate length by attaching it to the free surface of the module to bring its first natural frequency to 24.5 Hz as shown in Fig. 3(b). We conducted an experiment in a lab-scale water bath in which the rate of water flow was nearly constant. A water flow rate of 1.2 m/s on average was chosen and implemented with an electric pump. We selected a 1.2 $\mathrm { m } / \mathrm { s }$ of water flow to check the possibility of a practical application in the Han River (Seoul, South Korea) whose average annual water flow rate is $1 . 2 \mathrm { m } / \mathrm { s }$ . The water flow rate is constantly changing, however, setting the system to an average value is a way to achieve the maximum cumulative output energy. This is because the closer to the natural frequency of the module, the higher the output, even if it is not accurately frequency matched. Figure 4(a) presents a schematic design of a water bath that emulates a real underwater environment, such as a river. There is a water bath (size: $\mathrm { 7 0 0 ~ \times ~ 1 , 0 0 0 ~ \times ~ 6 0 0 ~ m m ^ { 3 } }$ ) which has an inlet and an outlet. Figure 4(b) shows a photo of the water bath. Figure 4(c) displays the concrete design of the propeller-based underwater piezoelectric energy harvesting system which consists of a propeller, hitting sticks and a piezoelectric module. The pumped water makes the propeller with a radius of 25 cm rotate with four hitting sticks connected through the rotating axis. These hitting sticks continuously strike the piezoelectric module and generate electricity. The flow of water whose direction is perpendicular to the propeller rotates the propeller in one direction, which makes the hitting sticks spin together. The hitting sticks strike the piezoelectric module continuously as long as the water flows through the propeller, thereby generating electricity. The rotating axis is held by three bearings. Two of the bearings are placed at the top of the rotating axis holder and the other one is placed between the axis and the wall of the waterproof box. Both the rotating axis holder and the box are firmly fixed to the bottom of the water bath as is the piezoelectric module holder. Figure 4(d) exhibits the experimental setup of the PU-PEH system. The propeller was installed 2.5 cm to the left, 27.5 cm from the inlet where the water flow rate is continuously 1.2 m/s (the water flow rate of the Han River) in Fig. 4(e). sections.heading: III. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
sections.text:
Figure 5(a) shows the open-circuit voltage of model $\# 3$ according to the number of hitting sticks (1–6). To ensure reliability, we performed three trials for each number of hitting sticks expressed in the inset. Because the hitting frequency varied with the number of hitting sticks, a power generation characteristics test was performed.

According to the number of hitting sticks, hitting sticks were placed at equal intervals ( $1 = 3 6 0 ^ { \circ }$ , $2 = 1 8 0 ^ { \circ }$ , 3 $= 1 2 0 ^ { \circ }$ , $4 = 9 0 ^ { \circ }$ , $5 = 7 2 ^ { \circ }$ and $6 = 6 0 ^ { \circ }$ ), and the maximum open-circuit voltage was about 50 V and the next high voltage of 44.5 V occurred with two hitting sticks. For four hitting sticks, the resonance frequency of model #3 matched the hitting frequency of 24.5 Hz and so it generated the highest power. For two hitting sticks, as described in our previous work [26], we interpreted the phenomena as synchronous resonance. This means that there was a phenomenon similar to resonance matching when the inverse proportion of the integer of the first resonance frequency was proportional in the equation as below.

$$
f _ { \mathrm { n } } = \frac { 1 } { n } f _ { \mathrm { r e s } } ( n = 1 , 2 , 3 \cdots )
$$

Therefore, the two hitting sticks generated a relatively high output voltage because they created a hitting frequency of about 12.35 Hz, half of the resonance frequency of model #3. Figure 5(b) displays the waveform of model $\# 3$ when hit by four hitting sticks. It shows the maximum output voltage of 50 V. An output power test of models $\# 1$ , $\# 3$ , #6 was carried out along matching impedances to determine the relationship between the bending length and the output power of the PU-PEH in Fig. 5(c). Model #3 which has the most similar resonance frequency with a hitting frequency of 24.7 Hz shows the highest output power of 17 mWrms at a resistance of $1 0 . 8 \ \mathrm { k } \Omega$ . Model $\# 1$ shows $1 1 ~ \mathrm { m W _ { r m s } }$ at a resistance of $1 3 . 8 ~ \mathrm { k } \Omega$ , and model $\# 6$ generates 9.8 mWrms at an $8 . 2 ~ \mathrm { k } \Omega$ matching impedance. Looking at trends, the order of higher resonance frequencies is 6, 3, and 1, and the order of higher matching resistance is the opposite. This can be explained by the following relationship.

$$
M a t c h i n g \ I m p e d a n c e = \frac { 1 } { j w C } = \frac { 1 } { j 2 \pi f C } ,
$$

where $w$ is the angular frequency, $f$ is the resonance frequency and $C$ is the capacitance of a piezoelectric module. Figure 5(d) shows the output power of all the models. Model $\# 3$ generated the maximum output power of $1 7 ~ \mathrm { m W _ { r m s } }$ (power density: 57.4 mW/cm3) and next, model $\# 4$ generated $1 6 . 2 \mathrm { \ m W _ { r m s } }$ (power density: 54.7 mW/cm3), which is the second highest power because of a resonance frequency (25.84 Hz) similar to the hitting frequency (24.7 Hz). Considering the volume of the piezoelectric material, the output power per density was calculated as $5 7 . 4 ~ \mathrm { m W / c m ^ { 3 } }$ , which is one of the highest values in the field of piezoelectric energy harvesting [13]. Finally, the energy generated by model #3 successfully turned on and off 972 LEDs as shown in the inset of Fig. 5(d).

In addition to the autonomous LED light system using PU-PEH that we demonstrated in this work, a reliable power supply system for the transmission of wireless sensor node data is a very important technology for ships.

![](images/25d412cde45829d038c29e23dd1dd8bb6453551cf0a41f70df25e17d38fd37dd.jpg)  
Fig. 6. (Color online) Block diagram of an autonomous obstacle detection system operated by the PU-PEH under water.

One such system is an obstacle detection system that keeps the ship safe from obstacles. Ships on the sea are always in danger from invisible obstacles in the sea, such as an iceberg. Therefore, a system that can detect and avoid these obstacles is essential. Previously, necessary power, such as a battery, was directly supplied to all underwater sensors, but it is absolutely necessary to introduce a self-powered system because it may not be possible to operate the sensors if there is a battery discharge. The PU-PEH system is self-generated by the propeller under water. Then, the output voltage is rectified and converted to DC, and it is converted into the operation voltage of a sensor (ultrasonic sensor) by a step-down converter as in Fig. 6. Measured obstacle data from the underwater sensor is transmitted to the obstacle data receiver in the ship so that the ship can avoid obstacles in front of the ship. The system is based on independent power sources that provide safety from obstacles even when there are problems with the power supply.

sections.heading: IV. CONCLUSIONS
sections.text: We designed and manufactured a piezoelectric energy harvesting system for generating energy from a fluid flow. It was designed to be operated in the Han River of Seoul in South Korea whose water runs at an average rate of $1 . 2 ~ \mathrm { m / s }$ . The running water rotates the propeller of the system to run four hitting sticks which exert force to the piezoelectric module at a frequency of 24.5 Hz. The first natural frequency of the piezoelectric module is also set to the exciting frequency using a frequency matching method to give the maximum performance. We determined the optimum condition for the piezoelectric module to be a bending length of 80 mm, which gives a maximum output power of 17 mW in a RMS value at a resistance of $1 0 . 8 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ . Thus, the power density was calculated to be 57.4 mW/cm $^ { 3 }$ , which is one of the highest records of piezoelectric energy harvesting. With our novel piezoelectric energy harvesting system for fluid flow, we successfully lit 972 LEDs using only one piezoelectric module. This paper confirmed the potential and feasibility of applying a piezoelectric energy harvesting system to a real underwater environment. Especially, the newly applied frequency tuning method using an acrylic plate will bring the advantages of mass product and better sustainability because the system doesn’t need to change a dimension of a piezoelectric device in various frequency conditions and also, the previous tip mass method results in vulnerability of a piezoelectric device from pre-strain. The proposed method achieves remarkable results in the field of piezoelectric energy harvesting using fluid flow. This method can serve as a ubiquitous autonomous energy source that converts mechanical energy from fluid flow into usable electrical energy for electronic applications such as light and ultrasonic sensors under water.
